cards.heading: Outcome versus proxy metrics defined
cards.question: What is the distinction between outcome and proxy metrics for an agent?
cards.answer: Proxy metrics (latency, cost, tool-call counts, error counts) fall out of the agent's own record; outcome evidence that the work was actually accomplished must come from artifacts the agent did not author, like a passing CI test, a merged PR, or a deploy that wasn't rolled back.

cards.heading: Why self-reported completion isn't measurement
cards.question: Why can't an agent's own claim of task completion count as an outcome signal?
cards.answer: The claim is produced by the very process whose success is in question — an agent whose objective is to finish will happily report finishing, so self-report is a claim, not a measurement.

cards.heading: Why outcome anchors must sit outside the agent
cards.question: Why do outcome anchors like merge status and CI results have to originate outside the agent's authorship?
cards.answer: Because they need to be cheap to read and expensive to fake — an anchor the agent could influence or generate itself provides no real evidence its work succeeded.

cards.heading: What proxy metrics can and can't catch
cards.question: What can proxy metrics reliably catch, and what can't they tell you?
cards.answer: They reliably catch runaway cost and loops that never terminate, but say nothing about whether the work produced was any good.

cards.heading: The recommended logging default
cards.question: What is the recommended default for how agent session data should be logged?
cards.answer: Verbose, append-only, structured as JSON lines — keep everything and trim later, since losing the inputs to a session with an unexplained outcome costs far more than the storage bill.
